This paper introduces the Time-Varying Poisson AutoRegressive with eXogenous covariates (TV-PARX) model, a novel econometric framework designed for modeling and forecasting count time series. We demonstrate that the score-driven approach is ideal for tracking the evolution of time-varying parameters, offering the necessary flexibility to handle count data with complex nonlinear dynamics and structural breaks. Under mild conditions, we establish the asymptotic properties of the TV-PARX model, proving that maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) produces parameter estimates that are both strongly consistent and asymptotically normal. Monte Carlo simulations are used to assess finite-sample performance and forecasting precision. Furthermore, the practical value of the TV-PARX model's time-varying specification is illustrated through an analysis of daily new COVID-19 infections in Italy and corporate defaults in the United States. To facilitate research in this area, an open-source R package named 'tvparx' has been developed to implement this new modeling approach for count time series. This initiative aims to replace traditional linear models, which often fail to capture the nonlinear characteristics inherent in count time series, with more appropriate methodologies. The potential applications of this work span economics, finance, and operations management.
Although the concept of employing stellar photometry to monitor the atmosphere for high-energy astrophysics optical experiments appears simple, achieving the high precision required to determine vertical aerosol optical depth (VAOD) to within 0.01 has been challenging. Wide-field photometry spanning various altitudes enables a rapid, calibration-independent VAOD calculation, while simultaneously serving as a valuable calibration by-product. By leveraging multi-year datasets from the FRAM (F/(Ph)otometric Robotic Atmospheric Monitor) telescope at the Pierre Auger Observatory in Argentina and approximately one year of data from a comparable instrument at the future Cherenkov Telescope Array site in Chile, we have refined measurement techniques to enhance precision. This analysis incorporates a detailed error budget, examines systematic effects, and utilizes a probabilistic approach to eliminate outliers caused by unrecognized errors. When combined with morning and evening calibration references, this "blind" method has proven effective for refining VAOD estimates, although it demands extensive datasets. For the FRAM telescope, this hybrid strategy yielded a precision of 0.006 VAOD, representing an improvement of a factor of 1.6 over the conventional calibration-only method using the same dataset. In this document, we outline this approach, validate it through simulations, and provide a comprehensive budget of uncertainties and systematic effects. We also discuss the necessary conditions, potential limitations, and a roadmap for implementing this technique as a standard practice, particularly in preparation for the Cherenkov Telescope Array.

For harmonic oscillators, specific schemes yield exact configurational averaging, potentially enhancing the modeling of biomolecules where bond stretching is critical. Consequently, the reliability of both the systems and their evaluation hinges on the quality of these reference descriptions. I contend that more detailed guidelines are necessary, ones that balance the specific requirements of visually impaired users with the practical feasibility of generating appropriate descriptions. While high-quality data would allow for reference-based evaluation, we should also explore alternative assessment methods. These could involve comparing systems based on their ability to prioritize user needs or determining which descriptions best support specific tasks, rather than relying solely on similarity against reference data. The reliability of visual recognition systems relies heavily on the quality of the data used for training, evaluation, and optimization. Given that deep learning methods have become increasingly accessible, it is now feasible to process enormous datasets to compile comprehensive lists of image descriptions. These datasets could significantly enhance the accuracy of image classification and segmentation approaches. Furthermore, large-scale image description datasets would enable a more valid form of evaluation for automatic image captioning. There is no doubt that such a dataset would be incredibly valuable for evaluating how well visually impaired users are served, potentially transforming this field. Unfortunately, as highlighted in Section 2, no such dataset currently exists. Creating one would be a substantial undertaking, but it remains possible. In this paper, I outline the challenges involved and propose a feasible approach. I also sketch out a framework for evaluating image captioning using this potential dataset, offering guidelines on how to assess the utility of systems for visually impaired users most effectively. Finally, I suggest methods for optimizing image description systems to better meet the needs of these users. It is time to make image captioning open-source and subject it to rigorous testing. Such an initiative would yield numerous benefits, including more valid evaluation metrics, improved validation of automatic image description systems, better service for visually impaired users, and enhanced training data
Quantifying complexity within quantum field theory remains a formidable challenge, primarily due to the difficulty of moving past free models and their associated Gaussian states and operations. Our approach addresses this by examining conformal field theories in 1+1 dimensions, offering a comprehensive analysis of complexity for both states and operators within the universal sector of their energy-momentum tensor. Central to our framework are the Euler-Arnold equations and their integro-differential extensions, which ensure the optimization problem between arbitrary states or transformations is well-defined. This work expands upon the findings detailed in arXiv:2005.02415, elaborating on the derivation techniques employed. Key areas of focus include the application of differential regularization, solving the integro-differential equation governing Fubini-Study state complexity, and investigating the underlying geometric structure. Furthermore, we define a novel operator complexity measure based on a geometric framework and compare two methods for regularizing this approach. Additional findings cover the behavior of state complexity under stretching and squeezing transformations, the emergence of plateau structures in time-dependent scenarios, and the development of a unified framework that incorporates freezing transformations. Finally, we establish a lower bound aligned with the Fermi speed limit and explore the geometric characteristics of the resulting extremal surface.

This research conducts a linear analysis of a turbulent methane-air jet flame to forecast how the reacting flow responds to upstream acoustic actuation. Within a linearized framework, capturing heat release fluctuations is essential for studying thermoacoustic instabilities and flame noise. Distinct from prior work, this study employs an active flame approach, which incorporates heat release oscillations induced by acoustic fluctuations. Implementing this approach linearly requires linearizing a combustion model; however, linearizing Large Eddy Simulation (LES) and Direct Numerical Simulation (DNS) models creates closure issues, rendering them difficult to apply in this context. Conversely, Reynolds-averaged Navier Stokes (RANS) models effectively avoid these problems, making them ideal for this application. These RANS models were linearized around the temporal mean flow of the turbulent jet, which was derived using LES. An open-loop linear system was formulated to estimate the traveling flame helicity (FH) mode and its associated oscillation frequency linearly. This estimation was achieved through a Graftak (GR) optimization method applied to linear responses (RBFs) to upstream acoustic actuation. The predicted FH mode frequency was verified against small-amplitude thermal response modes extracted from Direct Numerical Simulation (DNS). Furthermore, the linear estimate of the firing amplitude linearly matched the RBF of the DNS at various amplitudes. Ultimately, this study demonstrates that RANS models, linearized around the turbulent jet's mean flow, effectively describe oscillations in the turbulent jet flame linearly, even at large amplitudes where non-linear effects become significant.
Nonlocal gravity (NLG) represents a classical, nonlocal extension of Einstein's gravitational theory, modeled after the analogy with nonlocal electrodynamics in media. Within this framework, historical dependence is introduced through a constitutive relation that utilizes a causal kernel, which must ultimately be derived from observational data. This paper aims to reformulate nonlocal gravity so that the nonlocal components of the constitutive relation directly link measurable quantities, mirroring the approach found in nonlocal electrodynamics. The derived constitutive relation aligns with a recent proposal by Puetzfeld, Obukhov, and Hehl [25]. Utilizing this updated constitutive relation for NLG, it is demonstrated that de Sitter spacetime does not constitute a valid solution. Furthermore, the constitutive relation is employed to analyze planetary orbits around a mass, showing that such trajectories deviate from Newtonian expectations due to nonlocal effects; specifically, a weaker attraction is predicted for outer planets, potentially offering a solution to the galaxy rotation curve problem without invoking dark matter. These findings indicate that the previously proposed constitutive relation by Puetzfeld, Obukhov, and Hehl [25] for NLG yields counterintuitive outcomes regarding planetary motion, a issue shared by other nonlocal generalizations of general relativity. Finally, the constitutive relation serves as a basis for proposing a new method to estimate the kernel within the NLG model, likely from astronomical observations, analogous to how the kernel in nonlocal electrodynamics is determined from particle physics experiments. This estimation strategy may help resolve the criticism regarding the potential of the nonlocal constitutive relation to be derived a priori from empirical evidence. Notably, this paper focuses exclusively on the constitutive relation between stress-energy and curvature tensors, leaving the derivation of the updated field equations for future work.
This presentation reports on selected recent LHC findings from the ALICE, ATLAS, and CMS experiments concerning small systems. Given that the study of high-multiplicity QCD in small systems has become a rapidly expanding area of significant interest to both the heavy-ion and broader high-energy physics communities, it is not feasible to cover all related topics in this paper. Instead, the discussion will focus on measurements addressing collective phenomena in small systems and recent results on strangeness enhancement in proton-proton collisions. Readers should be aware that many other intriguing results were excluded from this discussion due to space constraints. As an entire review of small systems cannot be comprehensively covered here, relevant references can be found in the works cited in this introduction as well as in other recent reviews dedicated to small systems [1, 2].
The detection of certain variable X-ray sources in the Galactic Centre that have not exhibited outbursts over a ten-year monitoring period has led to the hypothesis of a substantial population of stellar-mass black holes in this area. A fundamental premise of this argument is the assertion that neutron stars in low-mass X-ray binaries (LMXBs) do not experience long intervals between transients. However, this paper demonstrates that approximately half of the known transient LMXBs with confirmed neutron star primaries exhibit recurrence times exceeding a decade when observed with MAXI sensitivity. Furthermore, we show that to align the expected total number of neutron star LMXBs with both current observations and the galaxy's millisecond radio pulsar population, the dominant class of these systems must have recurrence times far surpassing a century for MAXI-detectable outbursts, implying that few such systems have been identified to date. Finally, we argue that future searches for neutron star LMXBs could be significantly enhanced by targeting regions of the sky already known to contain black hole X-ray transients.

Bipartite graphs represent the connections between two separate sets of entities. These structures are frequently depicted in a two-tiered layout, where each entity set is shown as a collection of vertices aligned on one of two parallel horizontal lines, and their relationships are illustrated by edges linking corresponding vertices across the lines. A primary goal in creating such visualizations is to reduce edge crossings; however, minimizing crossings is computationally demanding and often yields drawings with so many intersections that they compromise readability. This work examines a recent method for eliminating crossings by splitting vertices, aiming to identify the minimum number of vertices that must be split to achieve a planar representation. We demonstrate that deciding whether a planar drawing is achievable by splitting at most $k$ vertices is fixed parameter tractable with respect to $k$. Furthermore, assuming the standard conjecture that problems are polynomial in both dimensions and fixed parameters, we establish that this problem is strictly hierarchy parameterized by $k$. Finally, we explore the feasibility of achieving planarity through the splitting of exactly one vertex, providing an optimal solution and analyzing its geometric properties.
Performance degradation techniques serve as a crucial complement to side-channel attacks. This study introduces HyperDegrade, a novel method that integrates prior strategies with simultaneous multithreading (SMT) architectures. Beyond this new technique, we identify a previously unrecognized source of slowdown by analyzing cache eviction as a root cause. The resulting performance degradation is substantially greater than previous methods, thereby enhancing the time granularity available for Flush+Reload attacks. We evaluated HyperDegrade across various Intel microarchitectures, achieving significant slowdowns that, in specific microbenchmark scenarios, represent a three-order-of-magnitude improvement over state-of-the-art solutions. To assess the effectiveness of performance degradation in amplifying side channels, we introduced and validated specific leakage metrics. Our findings indicate that HyperDegrade improves time granularity without compromising trace quality. Furthermore, we conducted a fair comparison of three performance degradation strategies when paired with Flush+Reload from an attacker's viewpoint. We also devised an attack targeting an underutilized vulnerability in OpenSSL, where HyperDegrade demonstrated superior performance by reducing the number of required Flush+Reload traces needed for success by a factor of three. In terms of cryptographic contributions, we revisited the recently proposed Raccoon attack on TLS-DH key exchanges, extending its application to other protocols. Leveraging HyperDegrade, we constructed an end-to-end attack proving that Raccoon-like exploits can succeed with real data, addressing a gap left by earlier research. Finally, we constructed a similar attack for Countermeasures-DH, analyzing how performance degradation influences the specificity of the resulting vulnerability. These end-to-end attacks utilize HyperDegrade; consequently, their efficacy varies based on the intensity of the induced performance slowdown, which depends on specific microarchitectural parameters. Given that our slowdown technique relies on cache eviction, it is most effective on systems with smaller cache sizes, whereas larger caches yield fewer slowdown benefits. Our investigation into HyperDegrade offers valuable insights into SMT microarchitectures and their exploitation, while also highlighting the interconnections between different microarchitectural features and potential vulnerabilities. These findings underscore the necessity of designing robust cryptographic protocols that remain secure even when supported by weaker performance degradation methods. An unknotting operation represents a local modification applied to knot diagrams. It is possible to convert any knot diagram into a trivial unknot diagram through a combination of unknotting operations and Reidemeister moves. These operations hold substantial significance in knot theory, particularly for analyzing knot complexity and invariants. Furthermore, they play a crucial role in fields such as biology, chemistry, and physics, where they help investigate the complex entanglements found in strings, organic molecules, and DNA. This paper introduces a novel unknotting operation known as the diagonal move, applicable to both classical and welded knots. We demonstrate that the crossing change, Delta-move, Sharp-move, Gamma-move, n-gon move, pass move, and 4-move can all be achieved via sequences of diagonal moves. Additionally, we define a distance metric based on the diagonal move and examine its characteristics. Finally, we calculate the diagonal move distances for various knots and curves, offering new findings regarding the unknotting value and related invariants. The concept of unknotting operations was initially proposed by Rasheed and Usman in \cite{RU18}, with further developments documented in \cite{RU19,RU20}.
Coordination serves as a vital capability in multi-agent systems, enabling the completion of objectives that single agents cannot achieve alone. This study examines how a team of strategic agents selects among multiple tasks within a stochastic framework, specifically focusing on two tasks with randomly distributed and partially observable difficulties. We demonstrate that when prior distributions regarding task difficulty are diffuse, a Nash equilibrium with a straightforward, intuitive linear structure emerges. Conversely, we find that if the prior distribution is not diffuse, an agent's best response to an affine strategy profile may become nonlinear. Furthermore, we present an algorithm capable of efficiently calculating a data-driven Nash equilibrium restricted to the class of affine policies. Finally, we highlight that both the affine policy class and the Data-Nash equilibrium concept are valuable for addressing scalability challenges in problems involving continuous state and action spaces. Notably, the affine policy class allows for a fixed number of parameters independent of state space size, while the Data-Nash concept requires storage only for a count of data points rather than an explicit data table. To validate these findings, the authors develop an empirical method for estimating affine policies and apply this approach to a task allocation scenario based on the divide-and-conquer philosophy. This scenario involves two assignable tasks and a team of homogeneous agents operating under a randomized rendezvous protocol, with the specific challenge of determining the optimal rendezvous location. As the empirical sample size grows, this estimated data-Nash policy converges toward the optimal Bayesian-Nash policy. Additionally, we outline future research directions concerning empirical policies derived from larger data sets. Overall, this work represents an empirical investigation into Nash equilibria, contrasting it with the more conventional theoretical approach found in standard game theory literature. Regarding the specific goal of optimizing task execution time, this optimization concern is integrated directly into the process of estimating the empirical policy from available data sets. While this paper assumes a team formulation where payoffs are defined as task execution times, similar investigations into Nash equilibria can be conducted using utility functions based on QoS metrics, such as energy efficiency [10], [11] or throughput [12], [13]. Similarly, while this work focuses on a team of homogeneous strategic agents, extensions to heterogeneous teams are feasible, though such investigations fall beyond the scope of this current research.

The high-frequency sensitivity of gravitational-wave detectors is constrained by quantum shot noise and ultimately by optical losses within the signal-recycling cavity. This limitation represents a primary barrier to detecting gravitational waves from binary neutron star mergers in both current and future detectors, as it remains independent of arm length and the level of injected squeezing. In this study, we propose a sloshing Sagnac interferometer topology, derived from a Michelson interferometer by optically linking the end mirrors to form an additional cavity. This configuration creates a triply-coupled cavity system capable of surpassing the loss-induced high-frequency limit inherent to signal-recycled Michelson interferometers. Using parameters comparable to advanced LIGO+, a sloshing-Sagnac design could achieve sevenfold improved sensitivity at 2.5 kHz, or a fourfold increase in signal-to-noise ratio for typical post-merger binary neutron star waveforms. As an evolution of the Michelson architecture, the sloshing-Sagnac interferometer offers a viable topology for upgrading current detectors and for future-generation observatories.

Extra-large scale massive multiple-input multiple-output (XL-MIMO) systems represent a promising solution for delivering ultra-high data rates in environments with high user density. Because the physical dimensions of XL-MIMO arrays are comparable to the distances separating them from user equipments (UEs), the system experiences spatial non-stationarities and distinct visibility regions (VRs). These factors, combined with high UE density and limited pilot resources, make the design of random access (RA) protocols and scheduling algorithms particularly difficult. This paper introduces a joint RA and scheduling approach called the non-overlapping VR XL-MIMO (NOVR-XL) protocol. This method leverages the unique VRs of individual UEs to enhance RA performance and prioritizes scheduling UEs with non-overlapping VRs within the same payload data pilot resource. Simulation results demonstrate that this proposed scheme yields substantial improvements in sum rate compared to conventional RA methods, while also lowering access latency and overall connectivity performance. Furthermore, the NOVR-XL approach exhibits resilience to errors in channel state information (CSI) estimation. Finally, these performance gains remain consistent even when the system scale is reduced. These findings indicate that the NOVR-XL method is well-suited for ultra-high data rate environments, such as city centers, large venues, and vehicles. Additionally, the concept can be applied to improve 5G New Air (5G-NA) satellite communications and vehicle-to-everything (V2X) systems. Notably, these benefits offer a potential solution to challenges faced by conventional cellular networks in urban areas and on highways. To facilitate these gains, NOVR-XL depends on ultra-large scale deployments, advanced signal processing capabilities, and AI-driven CSI estimation techniques. An open-source implementation of this scheme is available at the following GitHub link: https://github.com/NOVR-XL/NOVR-XL-System.
Although neural language models have largely replaced traditional $N$-gram models due to superior performance, our findings suggest that $N$-grams still yield satisfactory results in many scenarios, effectively capturing significant linguistic knowledge at a low computational cost. Leveraging this insight, we propose training a neural model to predict the residuals between an $N$-gram model and the actual data distribution. A graph $G=(V,E)$ equipped with geodesic distance $d(\cdot,\cdot)$ is considered resolved by a non-empty vertex subset $R$ if, for every pair of vertices $u$ and $v$, the condition $d(u,r)=d(v,r)$ holding for all $r\in R$ implies $u=v$. The metric dimension of $G$ corresponds to the size of its minimal resolving set. This manuscript introduces and examines the concepts of resolvability and metric dimension under a truncated geodesic distance defined by a threshold $k$, utilizing the metric $d_k(u,v):=\min\{d(u,v),k+1\}$. We define the metric dimension of $G$ relative to $d_k$ as $\beta_k(G)$. The study analyzes how $\beta_k(G)$ varies with respect to $k$ and the graph's diameter. Furthermore, we characterize the truncated metric dimension for paths, cycles, and graphs exhibiting extreme dimensions, specifically those of order $n$ where $\beta_k(G)=n-2$ or $\beta_k(G)=n-1$. The work concludes with an exploration of several issues concerning the truncated metric dimension of trees. Notably, we establish that $ \beta_k(T_1 \vee T_2 ) = \beta_k(T_1 ) + \beta_k(T_2 ) $ for disjoint trees $T_1$ and $T_2$, and we characterize those graphs $G$ for which $\beta_k(G)(\beta(G)-1)^{-1} \leqslant n(\beta(G)-1)^{-1}$. Finally, the manuscript examines this number in relation to cliques, complete multipartite graphs, and graphs with at most three edges. Our findings indicate that this number depends on the class definition, the threshold $k$, and the total vertex count $n$. It remains uncertain if bulge expansion causes the flattening of the star-forming main sequence (MS) at high masses. However, above $M_{\ast}=10^{10.2}M_{\sun}$, the central NUV$-r$ becomes significantly redder than the outer regions, indicating that bulges in massive galaxies are more evolved. When sorting galaxies by S\'ersic index $n$, those with $n$>2.0 exhibit redder central NUV$-r$ colors than those with $n$<2.0, even when controlling for B/T ratio and $M_{\ast}$. Furthermore, the fraction of galaxies with $n$>2.0 rises sharply with mass for $M_{\ast}>10^{10.2}M_{\sun}$, aligning with the turnover in the MS at this transition mass. While numerous reconstruction methods exist—from conventional protocols to machine learning approaches—no single universal technique currently allows for extracting the Wigner function from the optical tomogram of an arbitrary light state. We demonstrate that nonclassical phenomena, including entanglement variations during dynamical evolution and the emergence of quantum synchronization, manifest as qualitative shifts within the optical tomograms themselves. Consequently, explicit state reconstruction is unnecessary to detect these effects. Furthermore, we show that the Wigner function can be extracted directly from the optical tomogram via a specific formula tailored to the particular state under investigation. Additionally, we outline potential applications of this technique to other areas of quantum optics. Ultimately, our findings suggest that reconstruction-based nonclassicity measures, such as the Wigner negativity, should not be regarded as intrinsic properties of specific quantum states. Instead, they serve as practical tools for identifying and quantizing quantum features within defined subspaces of the overall Hilbert space.

This study tackles the persistent challenge of extracting dynamical information from noisy acoustic emission signals generated by an adhesive tape being peeled under a constant traction velocity. By applying a phase space reconstruction method, we confirm deterministic chaotic dynamics through the identification of a correlation dimension and a positive Lyapunov exponent within a specific range of traction speeds. These findings are interpreted using a model that underscores the deterministic nature of acoustic emissions by linking them to stick-slip dynamics. Notably, a fractal structure in the amplitude distribution of these emissions corresponds to the system's correlation dimension and its positive Lyapunov exponent. Consequently, the fractal characteristics of the amplitude distribution, the correlation dimension, and the Lyapunov exponent serve as equivalent indicators of deterministic chaos in this context. Finally, beyond the deterministic chaotic regime, a transition to stochasticity occurs as the correlation dimension loses meaning and the Lyapunov exponent becomes negative; this shift aligns with the system's amplitude distribution transitioning from fractal to Gaussian characteristics. The significance of the correlation dimension and Lyapunov exponent as markers for deterministic chaos versus stochastic behavior in noisy acoustic emission signals is further explored and compared with other relevant features. Additionally, these attributes offer valuable insights into the underlying mechanism producing these acoustic emissions, specifically the transition from stick-slip to continuous sliding dynamics. Space reconstruction serves as a crucial tool for analyzing the deterministic dynamics responsible for these acoustic releases.
In the early 1930s, K. Menger explored the concept of an abstract angle function, defining it broadly for metric and semi-metric spaces. He also formulated two challenges regarding the conformal embeddability of spaces equipped with an angle function into Euclidean spaces. Although these problems garnered attention later, solutions were limited to specific instances of metric spaces. This article updates the definition of the angle function to accommodate a broader class of spaces characterized by a betweenness relation, which we consider a more natural framework. Within this generalized setting, we resolve both problems originally posed by Menger. Furthermore, we establish the embeddability of spaces with this expanded angle function definition into Euclidean, Minkowski, and metric vector spaces, offering a comprehensive solution within this context. Additionally, we derive several properties of the angle function and its level sets, contributing to understanding how these spaces behave under composition and other operations. Our findings also clarify the relationship between the angle function and the notion of convexity along geodesics. Finally, we examine embeddability concerning the pair consisting of the angle function and distance, utilizing an example to demonstrate that this combination does not necessarily imply embeddability under the angle function alone. To conclude, we define a curvature function for spaces with an angle function, detailing its characteristics and connections to other concepts, before applying it to solve an open problem related to embeddability involving the angle function, betweenness, and dimension. As an additional contribution, we establish an inequality for the angle function analogous to the triangle inequality and explore its properties.

Fiber-reinforced composites featuring nanofiller-modified polymer matrices hold significant promise for enhancing the safety of high-risk engineering structures. These materials possess an inherent self-sensing capability, as their electrical conductivity alters in response to deformation and damage. This phenomenon, termed piezoresistivity, has been widely utilized for damage detection through electrical resistance measurements and tomographic imaging methods like electrical impedance tomography (EIT). While these approaches are highly effective at identifying the existence of damage, they struggle to deliver accurate details regarding the damage's shape, dimensions, or underlying mechanism. This limitation is especially problematic for laminated composites, which are prone to complex failure modes such as delaminations that are challenging to identify. To address this, we introduce a novel method for precisely determining the shape and size of damage in self-sensing composites. Our approach combines a genetic algorithm with realistic physics-based damage models to reconstruct accurate damage geometry from conductivity variations captured via EIT. We experimentally validated this technique using carbon nanofiber (CNF)-reinforced glass fiber-reinforced polymer (GFRP) laminates, focusing on two specific damage mechanisms: through-holes and delaminations. The results demonstrate that this new method can accurately reconstruct multiple through-holes with radii as small as 1.19 mm and delaminations resulting from low-velocity impacts. These findings indicate that integrating piezoresistivity with conductivity-based spatial imaging and physics-based inversion strategies can enable precise damage shape reconstruction in self-sensing composite structures. Such capability could significantly enhance safety by facilitating real-time health monitoring and supporting decision-making processes for structure-critical applications.

Advancements in technology have enabled big data processing, yet this has created substantial computational challenges when solving large-scale linear systems or performing matrix inversions. Consequently, there has been significant research into fast, approximate iterative methods for matrix inversion accelerated by Graphics Processing Units (GPUs), offering viable alternatives where traditional direct inversion methods are too costly. Existing techniques include the Neumann Series (NS), Newton iteration (NI), Chebyshev Iteration (CI), and Successive Over-Relaxation. This study introduces a novel iterative algorithm derived from the NS, termed "Nested Neumann" (NN). This approach generalizes higher-order iterations of NI and CI by leveraging a computationally efficient iterative update of the preconditioning matrix, dependent on a specified "inception depth." Mathematical analysis confirms that the NN method: (i) converges provided the preconditioning matrix satisfies the spectral norm condition required for NS, (ii) achieves a convergence rate equivalent to an order of (inception depth plus one), and (iii) performs optimally with an inception depth of one or two, contingent upon available RAM. Additionally, we derive an explicit formula for NN suitable for massive sparse matrices, accounting for increased computational costs. Crucially, we establish an analytical equivalence between NS and NN (including NI, CI, and higher orders), a finding particularly relevant for mMIMO systems. Finally, the NN method is applicable to positive semi-definite matrices for inversion and can be utilized for any linear system, whether sparse, non-sparse, or complex. Regarding direct inversion, we propose two variants of LU decomposition optimized for GPUs: LU with zero-block blocking (LU-0) and LU with sparse-block blocking (LU-S). Extensive numerical experiments using real-world big data matrices demonstrate that NN significantly outperforms NS, NI, CI, and the LU-based direct methods (LU-0 and LU-S) regarding speed. In specific scenarios, NN was approximately 2, 10, 20, and 30 times faster than NS, NI, CI, LU-0, and LU-S, respectively. These findings suggest NN is a highly effective technique for processing big data. Furthermore, the underlying iterative framework of NN can be adapted to other computationally intensive operations on large matrices. To facilitate broader adoption and comparison of matrix inversion strategies for big data, we have open-sourced the NN method along with a software package containing various configurations suitable for large-scale matrices, accessible at https://github.com/rajaji/NestedNeumann. While the VSI generates turbulence characterized by vigorous vertical motions that can influence dust accumulation and settling, dust evolution itself can suppress this instability. Specifically, as dust grows and settles, it depletes the gas, rendering cooling inefficient in the optically thin outer regions. This study employs linear analysis to quantify how dust evolution stabilizes the VSI. We developed a cooling timescale model incorporating dust growth beyond micron scales and size-dependent settling. By integrating this model with linear stability analysis, we identified the "VSI zone" and calculated the maximum growth rate at various radial distances. Our results indicate that both dust growth and settling restrict the VSI zone to the immediate vicinity of the midplane. Consequently, the instability's growth rate diminishes because the vertical shear of rotational velocity—the instability's driving force—is weaker at lower altitudes. In our default model of a 0.01 solar mass disk, dust growth from 10 microns to 1 mm reduces the growth rate by a factor exceeding 10. Ultimately, the suppression of VSI-driven turbulence by dust evolution could accelerate further dust processing in outer disk regions and account for the significant dust settling observed in the HL Tau system. Kinetical energy spectra and global mode analyses remain to be tested against these conclusions.

The rise of outsourced training and machine learning as a service has introduced new attack vectors, specifically backdoor attacks. These attacks conceal a secret function within a neural network that activates only when a specific trigger is present in the input. While most existing literature assumes static triggers with fixed locations and patterns—properties upon which many detection mechanisms rely—recent studies have demonstrated that image classification countermeasures like Neural Cleanse and ABS can be circumvented using dynamic triggers that remain effective regardless of their position or appearance. However, such dynamic backdoors are resource-intensive, typically requiring a significant portion of poisoned training data. This work presents the first demonstration that dynamic backdoor attacks can occur via a global average pooling layer without needing an increased volume of poisoned data. Despite this theoretical possibility, experimental results across sound classification, text sentiment analysis, and image classification indicate that implementing such attacks remains highly challenging in practice. These findings offer valuable insights for designing robust against both static and dynamic backdoors minimal modification detectors. Notably, this work confirms that multi-hot encoding of input locations serves as a meaningful feature for detecting dynamic backdoors, enabling effective detection even with minimal modified inputs, unlike other input properties. Aligned with the principle that one should not optimize for rare adversarial events, this research underscores the need for stronger alternatives to using modified inputs as a feature for identifying dynamic backdoor attacks.
This work addresses the challenge of a Parameter Server (PS) learning a model from data distributed across graph nodes, with Federated Learning (FL) serving as the primary application. A significant hurdle in FL is the communication bottleneck between nodes and the PS. Although performing multiple local updates per iteration before syncing with the PS is a common strategy to alleviate this bottleneck, the statistical heterogeneity of node-specific data often results in biased models and delayed convergence. To overcome both communication and data heterogeneity issues, we investigate Random Walk (RW) learning algorithms. These algorithms utilize direct connections between nodes, which are typically more efficient than communicating with the PS. In this framework, the model acts as a "baton" passed iteratively to a neighboring node after each update. Designing effective RW algorithms is complicated by data heterogeneity and uncertainty regarding data distributions; ideally, nodes with more informative data should be visited more frequently. We formulate this as a sleeping multi-armed bandit (MAB) problem to develop a near-optimal node sampling strategy that minimizes gradient estimate variance and asymptotically approaches optimal sampling. Building on this, we propose an adaptive random walk learning algorithm and provide theoretical convergence guarantees. Our numerical experiments confirm these theoretical results and demonstrate that our algorithm surpasses existing random walk methods. Furthermore, we conduct a real-world experiment using a FL implementation on Intel Ouia devices with a dictionary dataset, showing that our approach achieves faster convergence than traditional random walk methods and even certain centralization learning approaches. The source code for this real-world experiment is accessible at https://github.com/NingSui/Outia-Dict-FedAvg.
Pixel-level annotation scarcity remains a significant challenge in medical image segmentation. To address this, we present a novel regularization approach utilizing interpolation-based mixing for semi-supervised medical image segmentation. This method employs a consistency regularization strategy that ensures the segmentation of interpolated pairs of unlabeled images aligns with the interpolation of their corresponding segmentation maps. As a form of data-adaptive regularization, it helps reduce overfitting to labeled data, particularly when confidence levels are high. Compared to adversarial and generative models, this approach offers the advantage of requiring no extra computational resources. Evaluations on two public MRI datasets, ACDC and MMWHS, show that our method outperforms existing semi-supervised models. The source code is accessible at: https://github.com/hritam-98/ICT-MedSeg. Adversarial data has emerged as an effective technique for enhancing performance in computer vision tasks, serving either as a pre-processing step or as a regularization layer during training. In single-image medical segmentation, adversarial noise has been added to labels to help networks generalize better across different label distributions. However, in multi-image tasks like semi-supervised segmentation, such noise could degrade performance on unlabeled images. Furthermore, previous studies lack evaluation on real-world medical data with varying annotated proportions. To tackle these issues, we developed a content-adaptive regularization model based on pixel-level annotation density, integrated into semi-supervised medical image segmentation. Experiments on the ACDC and MMWHS datasets confirm that our approach significantly surpasses current state-of-the-art methods.
At the 1927 Solvay conference, Einstein proposed a thought experiment aimed at demonstrating the incompleteness of quantum mechanics by leveraging the instantaneous nonlocal consequences of wave function collapse—a phenomenon he termed "spooky action at a distance"—triggered by measurement. This event preceded the famous Einstein-Podolsky-Rosen critique. In this work, we utilize the Stern-Gerlach experiment to illustrate how the instantaneous nonlocal nature of wave function collapse, combined with single-particle entanglement, generates the nonlocal effect known as steering. During this process, Bob's quantum state becomes contingent upon the specific observable Alice chooses to measure. To achieve this, we fully harness the spatial spreading of the single-particle's entangled wave function over large distances. Specifically, we show that the nonlocality inherent in single-particle entanglement enables the particle to "know" which detector Alice employs to steer Bob's state. Consequently, despite significant counterarguments, we establish that single-particle entanglement produces genuine nonlocal effects across distant locations, thereby opening avenues for implementing truly nonlocal tasks using this phenomenon. Importantly, these effects do not violate the principle of no-signaling, as the actualized nonlocality resides within the entangled wave function itself rather than within the post-collapse local states. To utilize these genuine nonlocal features, we employ the instantaneous collapse of the entangled wave function as a resource, a strategy that distinguishes our approach from conventional strategies that rely on nonlocality between independently prepared states. Finally, we demonstrate that this resource can be harnessed to enable information coding within the entangled wave function and to violate Bell inequalities in a genuine nonlocal manner through the statistical analysis of sequences of truly nonlocal events. Additionally, we illustrate how the instantaneous nonlocal collapse of the entangled wave function can facilitate the resolution of the quantum Cheshire cat effect.

Nevertheless, their substantial model size hinders practical deployment, particularly in video recognition tasks involving high-dimensional data. Such comprehensive global analyses are indispensable for validating the model's completeness and identifying potential higher-scale physics connections, particularly through the seesaw mechanism. These analyses may even reveal a "second portal" to beyond-Standard-Model phenomena, complementing the traditional heavy Higgs exchange. Ultimately, our complete numerical framework enables the unification of neutrino mixing angles, masses, majorphilia-dominated direct dark matter detection signals, and see-saw suppressed semi-visible dark matter signals at future hadron colliders. We anticipate that this complete model, along with its public tutorials, will serve as a valuable resource for assessing the viability of natural dark sector models and assessing their testability at emerging high-energy colliders.
